source.grounding: help.splunk.com Splunk Enterprise 10.4, SPL Search Reference and Search Manual

questions.stem: What are the default values of `maxspan`, `maxpause` and `maxevents` on the `transaction` command?

options.text: maxspan -1, maxpause -1, maxevents 1000
options.explanation: maxspan and maxpause default to -1, which deactivates the constraint. maxevents is the only one of the three with a positive default.

options.text: maxspan 30s, maxpause 5m, maxevents 1000
options.explanation: These look like plausible time limits but neither time option has a positive default. Both are off unless you set them.

options.text: maxspan -1, maxpause -1, maxevents -1
options.explanation: Three deactivated constraints would let a transaction grow without bound. maxevents is capped at 1000 by default.

options.text: maxspan 1000, maxpause 1000, maxevents 1000
options.explanation: 1000 is the maxevents default only. The two time options are unset.

questions.overallExplanation: Only maxevents constrains a transaction by default, at 1000 events. A negative value on any of the three deactivates that constraint, so `maxevents=-1` means no event ceiling rather than no events.

guide.blueprintTitle: Group events using fields and time
guide.verdictNote: The 1000 is a per-search default, not a product ceiling. The real ceilings live in limits.conf as maxopentxn, default 5000, and maxopenevents, default 100000.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Option table with the defaults for maxspan, maxpause and maxevents.

questions.stem: A transaction groups exactly one event. What is its `duration`?

options.explanation: duration is the difference in seconds between the first and last event timestamps. With one event those are the same timestamp, so the difference is zero.

options.text: NULL, because a duration needs two events
options.explanation: The field is still produced. A single-event transaction has a real duration of zero rather than a missing one.

options.text: 1, counted as one event's worth of time
options.explanation: duration measures elapsed seconds, not events. Event count is reported separately in eventcount.

options.text: The event's `_time` value in epoch seconds
options.explanation: That would be an absolute timestamp rather than an elapsed span. duration is always a difference.

questions.overallExplanation: duration is in seconds, always, and is the span from the earliest to the latest member event. Convert with eval if you need minutes. The transaction's own `_time` comes from the earliest member event, not the latest.

guide.verdictNote: A duration of 0 across many rows usually means the search filtered on a term before grouping, so each group contains only the matching events.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: duration is the difference in seconds between the first and last events in the transaction.

questions.stem: Which option, when specified, causes `transaction` to set `closed_txn=1` on completed groups?

options.text: `startswith`
options.explanation: closed_txn is set when one of maxevents, maxspan, maxpause or startswith is specified. startswith is the one boundary option on that list.

options.text: `endswith`
options.explanation: endswith is deliberately absent from the documented list, which is what makes it the most common wrong answer here.

options.text: `keepevicted`
options.explanation: keepevicted decides whether unclosed transactions are output at all; it does not decide how closure is determined.

options.text: `unifyends`
options.explanation: unifyends governs whether events matching the start or end conditions are unified with the group, not closure marking.

questions.overallExplanation: The documented list is maxevents, maxspan, maxpause and startswith. If none of those four is given, every transaction is marked closed. endswith on its own does not qualify, despite reading like a closing condition.

guide.blueprintTitle: Group events using fields and time
guide.verdictNote: Pair this with keepevicted: transactions left open carry closed_txn=0 and are only returned when keepevicted=true.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: closed_txn is set to 1 only if one of maxevents, maxspan, maxpause or startswith is specified.

questions.stem: Why does `... | transaction clientip | where count > 5` return nothing?

options.text: transaction produces `eventcount`, not `count`.
options.explanation: count is what stats produces. The field that holds the number of events in a transaction is eventcount, so the filter references a field that does not exist.

options.text: where cannot be used after transaction.
options.explanation: where composes with transaction normally. The problem is the field name in the expression.

options.text: transaction only outputs `_raw` and `_time`.
options.explanation: It also adds duration and eventcount, sets closed_txn, and can add _txn_orphan and transactiontype.

options.text: count exists but is a string, so the numeric comparison fails.
options.explanation: The field is absent rather than mistyped. `where eventcount > 5` is the working form.

questions.overallExplanation: The two grouping commands name their count differently: stats gives count, transaction gives eventcount. Options such as maxspan, maxpause and maxevents are inputs only and never come back as fields.

guide.verdictNote: The full output contract: duration and eventcount always, closed_txn set, _txn_orphan only with keeporphans, transactiontype only when a configured transaction type is used.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: The command adds the fields duration and eventcount to each transaction.

questions.stem: A report needs one row per session with the session's event count, running against a large distributed deployment. Which command should be used, and why?

options.text: stats, because it is transforming and runs on the indexers
options.explanation: stats is a transforming command and performs more efficiently, especially in a distributed environment, because the work distributes across indexers.

options.text: transaction, because it produces fewer results
options.explanation: Result count is not the deciding factor, and transaction is a centralized streaming command that only runs on the search head.

options.text: transaction, because stats cannot count events per group
options.explanation: `stats count BY sessionid` does exactly that. Counting per group is stats' core job.

options.text: streamstats, because it is a cheaper stats
options.explanation: streamstats adds running aggregates to each event and returns every event. It never collapses events into groups.

questions.overallExplanation: Prefer stats unless you need something only transaction gives you: events physically grouped and kept, a span or pause constraint, or start and end conditions. The documentation recommends stats for performance in distributed environments.

guide.blueprintTitle: Determine when to use transactions vs. stats
guide.verdictNote: 3.6 is the only sub-objective in this section that is a judgement call rather than a recall fact, and it is weighted inside the heaviest section on the blueprint.

docs.title: About event grouping and correlation (Search Manual 10.4)
docs.note: stats is recommended over transaction for performance; transaction runs on the search head only.

questions.stem: Which pair of `stats` functions returns values in chronological order rather than processing order?

options.text: `earliest()` and `latest()`
options.explanation: These are the time-ordered pair. earliest() returns the chronologically oldest value and latest() the newest.

options.text: `first()` and `last()`
options.explanation: These follow processing order. Because results arrive newest first, first() usually returns the most recent value and last() the oldest, which is the reverse of what the names suggest.

options.text: `min()` and `max()`
options.explanation: These compare values, not timestamps. On a numeric field they return the smallest and largest numbers.

options.text: `list()` and `values()`
options.explanation: Both return collections rather than a single value. list() preserves event order and values() sorts lexicographically.

questions.overallExplanation: first() and last() are ordered by how results are processed, not by time. Use earliest() and latest() whenever the question is about chronology, which is most of the time in transaction reporting.

guide.verdictNote: The naming is genuinely counter-intuitive, which is exactly why it is examinable. Read first() as "first one processed", not "first in time".

docs.title: Statistical and charting functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: first() and last() are documented against processing order; earliest() and latest() against time.

options.text: values() returns distinct values sorted lexicographically; list() returns every value in event order and stops at 100.
options.explanation: Both parts matter. values() deduplicates and sorts, list() keeps duplicates and order but silently truncates at 100 values.

options.text: They are the same function under two names.
options.explanation: They differ in deduplication, ordering and whether a cap applies.

options.text: values() keeps duplicates; list() removes them.
options.explanation: This is exactly backwards. values() is the deduplicating one.

options.text: list() sorts lexicographically; values() preserves event order.
options.explanation: Also reversed. values() sorts, list() preserves order.

questions.overallExplanation: values() returns distinct values in lexicographical order with no documented cap. list() returns all values in the order the events arrived and returns only the first 100 if a field has more than 100 values.

guide.verdictNote: The 100-value cap on list() is the detail most often missed, and it makes list() unsafe for anything you intend to count.

docs.title: Statistical and charting functions (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: list() returns only the first 100 values of a field; values() returns distinct values in lexicographical order.

questions.stem: What is the default of `mvlist` on `transaction`, and what does that default produce?

options.text: false, rendering multivalue fields as a set of unique values in alphabetical order
options.explanation: With mvlist=false, which is the default, duplicate values collapse and the remaining values are ordered alphabetically.

options.text: true, rendering multivalue fields as the original event values in arrival order
options.explanation: That is what mvlist=true does, but it is not the default. You have to ask for it.

options.text: false, suppressing multivalue fields entirely
options.explanation: Nothing is suppressed. The values are deduplicated and sorted, not removed.

options.text: true, and it cannot be changed on a per-search basis
options.explanation: The default is false, and the option is settable per search like every other transaction option.

questions.overallExplanation: mvlist=false deduplicates and alphabetises. mvlist=true preserves the original values and their order, which is what you want when the sequence of events inside a transaction is the thing you are analysing.

guide.verdictNote: A related default to keep straight: unifyends inherits its default from connected, so setting connected=false also makes unifyends false.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: mvlist option, default false, controls unique-and-sorted versus original-order rendering.

questions.stem: What kind of value do `startswith` and `endswith` accept?

options.text: A search expression, a quoted search expression in parentheses, or `eval(<expression>)` returning a Boolean
options.explanation: These are the three documented filter-string forms. A regular expression is only usable inside the eval form, via match().

options.text: A regular expression, applied against `_raw`
options.explanation: They are not regex arguments. Getting regex behaviour requires wrapping it: `startswith=eval(match(_raw, "..."))`.

options.text: A field name whose presence opens or closes the transaction
options.explanation: A bare field name is not the documented form. The value is a filter expression, not a field reference.

options.text: An epoch timestamp marking the boundary
options.explanation: Time boundaries are the job of maxspan and maxpause, not of the start and end conditions.

questions.overallExplanation: The documented type is a filter-string. Plain search syntax works, parenthesised quoted search syntax works, and eval() with a Boolean expression works. Regex only reaches these options through eval(match(...)).

guide.blueprintTitle: Group events using fields and time
guide.verdictNote: Remember that specifying startswith affects closed_txn marking while specifying endswith does not.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: startswith and endswith take a <filter-string>, defined as search or eval syntax.

questions.stem: What is the difference between `keepevicted=true` and `keeporphans=true`?

options.text: keepevicted outputs transactions left open, marked `closed_txn=0`; keeporphans outputs events that joined no transaction, marked `_txn_orphan=1`.
options.explanation: Two different populations. Evicted means an incomplete group; orphaned means an event that never became part of any group.

options.text: They are two names for the same option.
options.explanation: They output different things and set different marker fields.

options.text: keepevicted keeps orphan events; keeporphans keeps unclosed transactions.
options.explanation: The two are swapped here.

options.text: keepevicted marks results with `orphan=1`; keeporphans marks them with `closed_txn=0`.
options.explanation: The marker fields are also swapped, and there is no field called orphan. The field is _txn_orphan.

questions.overallExplanation: Both default to false. keepevicted returns groups that memory pressure or a missing close condition left open, identifiable by closed_txn=0. keeporphans returns individual events that belonged to no transaction, identifiable by _txn_orphan=1.

guide.verdictNote: The underscore in _txn_orphan matters. Distractors routinely offer a plain orphan field, which does not exist.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: keepevicted and keeporphans option descriptions with their marker fields.

questions.stem: A search appends a second dataset and then needs to group the combined results by `sessionid`. What is the constraint?

options.text: transaction cannot be used after append; use stats to group instead.
options.explanation: This is a documented restriction. stats is the supported way to group after an append.

options.text: append cannot be followed by any transforming command.
options.explanation: stats, chart and timechart all work after append. The restriction is specific to transaction.

options.text: transaction works but silently ignores events from the appended set.
options.explanation: The combination is not supported rather than partially supported.

options.text: There is no constraint; the two compose freely.
options.explanation: They do not. This is one of the few explicit command-ordering restrictions in SPL.

questions.overallExplanation: transaction after append is not supported. This reinforces the general lesson of 3.6: stats is the more composable grouping command, and transaction is the special case you reach for only when you need its specific behaviour.

guide.blueprintTitle: Determine when to use transactions vs. stats
guide.verdictNote: transaction also requires its input in descending chronological order, so any sort has to sit immediately before it.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Usage: you cannot use the transaction command after the append command.

questions.stem: By default, how many subsearch results will `join` match against each main-search result?

options.explanation: join defaults to max=1, so only the first matching row from the right-hand dataset is used. `max=0` removes the limit.

options.text: All of them
options.explanation: That is the SQL expectation and the reason join surprises people. You have to set max=0 to get it.
There is no ten-row default on join. Ten is the default series limit on chart and timechart.
50,000 is the default maximum size of the right-hand dataset, not the number matched per row.

questions.overallExplanation: join is the correlation command most likely to give quietly wrong answers: max defaults to 1, the right-hand dataset is capped at 50,000 rows, and it has a default runtime limit of 60 seconds. The documentation recommends stats for most correlation work.

guide.verdictNote: Silent truncation is the danger. A join that returns too few rows looks like a data problem rather than a default.

docs.title: join command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: max default is 1; the subsearch is subject to result-count and runtime limits.

questions.stem: Which two behaviours require `transaction` rather than `stats`? (Choose two.)

options.text: Grouping events that must fall within a maximum elapsed span of each other
options.explanation: maxspan and maxpause have no equivalent in stats. Time-bounded grouping is transaction's distinctive capability.

options.text: Keeping the original events inside each group so their raw text stays available
options.explanation: transaction produces groups of events and preserves _raw. stats produces a statistics table and discards _raw.

options.text: Counting how many events share a field value
options.explanation: `stats count BY field` does this and does it faster, because stats distributes across indexers.

options.text: Producing one row per unique combination of two fields
options.explanation: That is exactly what `stats ... BY fieldA fieldB` produces, and it is the standard approach.

questions.overallExplanation: Reach for transaction when you need time constraints, start and end conditions, or the events themselves preserved as a group. For plain counting and aggregation by field value, stats is both simpler and faster.

guide.blueprintTitle: Determine when to use transactions vs. stats
guide.verdictNote: Because stats does not pass _raw down the pipeline, a later bare-keyword search after stats has nothing to match against.

docs.title: About transactions (Search Manual 10.4)
docs.note: When a transaction is the right tool versus aggregation with stats.

questions.stem: `... | transaction host cookie` is run. How does Splunk treat the two fields?

options.text: Not necessarily as a strict AND or OR; a transitive relationship across events can join them into one transaction.
options.explanation: The documentation states multiple fields are not necessarily interpreted as a conjunction or a disjunction. If a transitive relationship exists and events appear in the right sequence, transaction uses it.

options.text: As a strict conjunction: both host and cookie must match.
options.explanation: This is the intuitive reading and the documented warning is aimed precisely at it.

options.text: As a strict disjunction: either field matching is enough.
options.explanation: Equally definite and equally wrong. The behaviour is not fixed to either operator.

options.text: Only the first field is used; the second is ignored.
options.explanation: Both participate in grouping. Neither is discarded.

questions.overallExplanation: A multi-field transaction can chain events transitively: event 1 and 2 share a host, event 2 and 3 share a cookie, and all three end up in one transaction. This is why multi-field transactions can produce surprisingly large groups.

guide.verdictNote: This is the behaviour connected=false is designed to constrain, and connected is only relevant when a field or field list is specified.

docs.title: transaction command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Usage: multiple fields are not necessarily interpreted as a conjunction or disjunction; transitive relationships are used.
